title.narrative: EL PAcCTO 2.0 programme against transnational organised crime with LAC

description.narrative: Contract related to: EL PAcCTO 2.0 programme against transnational organised crime with LAC - EL PAcCTO 2.0 will be the largest programme supporting implementation of the Regional TEI for Justice and Security. As such, the intervention logic of the programme is aligned to the one of the Regional TEI co-created with the EU MS and European Institutions. The overall objective of this action is to establish an effective EU-LAC partnership on strengthening the rule of law and fight against organized crime, fostering citizen security and stability, both in LAC and in Europe. Based upon a `demand-driven¿ and `flexible geometry¿ approach, the programme will work towards three specific objectives: 1.    Consolidate and strengthen LAC regional and EU-LAC bi-regional structures and mechanisms for cooperation on justice and security matters;2.    Strengthen the LAC¿s overall rule of law environment and criminal justice system institutions¿ capacity to fight against transnational organised crime, including a focus on women and youth-specific concerns;3.    Address specific challenges of main transnational criminal markets of LAC organised crime (trafficking in drugs, arms, human beings and cultural goods; environmental and cyber-crimes).EL PAcCTO 2.0 includes two dedicated country windows for Mexico and Peru, reflecting the will to deepen the justice and security-related cooperation with those countries on issues of common interest on the basis of a successful policy dialogue with the European counterparts.Overall, the programme will contribute to the 2030 Agenda and its Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions, SDG 5: Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls and SDG 15: Life on land.

title.narrative: OC1.6. Number of regional and biregional political and technical mechanisms for cooperation on justice and security and penitentiary matters operational

description.narrative: The indicator will report on the number of active regional and biregional mechanisms for strategic, technical or operational cooperation on justice and security and penitentiary matters related to organized crime supported by the intervention. Regional and biregional political and technical mechanisms for cooperation should be understood as any formal structure or platform (i.e., formally established in a written document) that seeks to facilitate the exchange of information and good practices among countries and/or regional institutions to, ultimately, enhance coordination and cooperation when addressing common challenges. The indicator covers mechanisms that seek to facilitate the following types of cooperation: Strategic and political cooperation: for longterm planning and policy development, e.g., shared policy cycles, regional strategic exercises. Technical cooperation: including information sharing and exchange platforms, working groups, technical committees, regional training programmes. Operational cooperation: exchange of information and collaboration for operations in key criminal markets (i.e., police networks & working groups, SMTs, OTFs)The indicator requires the cooperation mechanism to be operational, i.e., activities (meetings, conferences, exchanges of information, development of guidelines or agreements) must have taken place during the implementation period.Only cooperation and information exchange mechanisms which were directly or indirectly supported by EL PACCTO 2.0 during the implementation period will be considered for the purpose of this indicator. The mechanisms should address cooperation on justice, security and penitentiary matters, with the ultimate aim of contributing to the fight against organized crime. They do not have to exclusively cover organised crime, but organised crime should be explicitly addressed by the cooperation mechanism during the implementation period to be included under this indicator.

title.narrative: OC1.2. Number of organized crimerelated investigations, operations, and cases jointly developed by LAC countries and/or with EU Member States

description.narrative: This indicator will quantify the number of organised crimerelated investigations, operations or cases jointly developed by LAC countries and/or with EU Member States, with support from the intervention. it will measure the support provided to joint LAC / LACEU efforts to fight organized crime, more specifically in the context of joint: Investigations: criminal investigations conducted by competent authorities within each country or countries to gather evidence to determine whether a crime has been committed and ascertain the methods, motives, and identities of criminals and the identity of victims and may also search for and interrogate witnesses. They are generally carried out by law enforcement agencies and specialized units. Operations: coordinated actions undertaken by law enforcement agencies or other relevant authorities to address / disrupt specific criminal activities or targets (i.e., apprehending suspects, seizing illicit assets or preventing criminal acts). The main difference with investigations is while investigations seek to gather information, operations involve action. Cases: these are specific instances in which criminal activities are investigated, prosecuted and adjudicated. Cases may originate from investigations conducted by law enforcement agencies but they are always prosecuted and adjudicated by judicial authorities (courts or tribunals). Criminal cases generally begin after the person is arrested and informed of their charges. Most criminal cases are tried by a judge in the presence of a jury, and may result in sentences under criminal law. Such sentences could include jail time as well as fines.The indicator only considers investigations / operations / cases supported by EL PACCTO 2.0, i.e., carried out by operational cooperation mechanisms / networks that were created or enhanced with support from EL PACCTO 2.0 or if the program was otherwise involved in the facilitation of operational contacts and exchange information.

Having strengthened the basis for operational cooperation during the first phase of EL PACCTO the second phase will make more emphasis on the operational pillar of the project which is expected to lead to a significant increase in the number of investigations operations and cases. The Colombian window is also expected to yield significant results under this indicator 10 operations per year can be expected.

title.narrative: OC1.5. Number of formal judicial requests presented between LAC countries and/or to EU Member States

description.narrative: The indicator will report on the number of formal judicial requests presented between LAC countries and/or to EU Member States, with support from the intervention. Formal judicial requests are structured, written communications between judicial authorities to facilitate legal processes across different jurisdictions. They rely on established legal frameworks and treaties to ensure compliance and effectiveness. Key elements of formal judicial requests include: Written format: it must be documented in writing, i.e., there has to be a clear and formal record of the communication. Judicial authority: it must originate from a competent judicial authority, such as a court, prosecutor, or magistrate. Legal basis: judicial requests are generally based on mutual legal assistance treaties (MLATs), conventions, or regional agreements. Specificity: The request should specify the nature of the assistance required, which may include gathering evidence, executing searches and seizures, serving legal documents, or extraditing individuals. Procedural Compliance: The request must comply with the legal and procedural requirements of both the requesting and requested jurisdictions. This includes adhering to deadlines, formalities, and any necessary translations. Direct Communication: The request is often transmitted directly between judicial authorities or through designated central authorities to ensure prompt and secure handling.For the purpose of this indicator, supported by EL PACCTO 2.0 requires that the formal judicial requests be channeled through EL PACCTO 2.0

comment.narrative: We expect that the foundation for judicial cooperation established during the first phase of the programme will translate in effective information exchanges between judicial authorities during the second phase. We expect that the information and support provided by EL PACCTO on MLA will translae into 12 formal judicial requests per year on average.

title.narrative: OC1.4. Number of highvalue organised crime targets identified, arrested, or prosecuted between LAC countries and/or with EU Member States

description.narrative: This indicator will measure the number of highvalue organised crime targets identified, arrested, or prosecuted between LAC countries and/or with EU Member States, with support from the intervention. It will seek to measure the success of joint operations supported by the intervention in apprehending highvalue targets. Referring to Europols definition, HVTs are individuals (or entities) whose capture or neutralisation is expected to have a significant impact on disrupting and dismantling criminal organisations. Investigations involving HVTs require more intensive support than standard priority cases, often including the development of comprehensive operational plans and the formation of Operational Task Forces to coordinate intelligence and investigation activities, including field operations. HVTs within Europols framework typically include:a. Leaders or Key Members: Individuals holding leadership positions or crucial roles within the criminal network.b. Financial Controllers: Those managing the financial operations, including money laundering and funding activities.c. Specialised Operatives: Individuals with unique skills essential to the criminal organizations operations.d. Key Facilitators: People who significantly aid in the logistics, coordination, or operational aspects of the criminal enterprise.Supported by EL PACCTO 2.0 implies that the HVTs have been identified / arrested / prosecuted through investigations (identified), operations (arrested) or cases (prosecuted) supported by EL PACCTO 2.0, as per indicator OC1.2.

comment.narrative: On avergae 23 HVTs identified 1 arrested and 1 prosecuted per year.

title.narrative: OP1.1.2. Number of strategic and policy dialogue processes on justice and security matters supported

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of strategic (policy or technical) dialogue processes on justice and security matters supported, covering highlevel processes (e.g., meetings, exchanges, platforms, exercises) which allow relevant stakeholders (policymakers, government representatives, civil society organizations, experts, practitioners, etc.) to raise and discuss common issues, share perspectives or develop a common vision. Ultimately, these may lead to concrete strategic and policy action to fight organized crime. The strategic dialogue processes aim at facilitating the identification of threats and establishment of longterm goals, priorities and strategies. For the purpose of these indicator, two types of strategic dialogue processes can be distinguished: Strategic policy dialogues, which involve policymakers. For reporting processes, this category only considers structured policy dialogue processes (currently CLASI and Justice Policy Cycle in LAC and the established dialogues with their EU counterparts). Strategic technical dialogue processes: this category covers other processes or mechanisms that allow for strategic exchanges among policymakers, sometimes also involving other key stakeholders (e.g., experts, practitioners, etc.). These can be structured or nonstructured / nonrecurrent. They may often support or be linked to strategic policy dialogues, but they involve specific dedicated activities. For instance, IDEAL, RAP or REDCOPEN.The processes should cover organized crime from a security (related to the actions adopted to prevent and investigate organized crime, i.e., law enforcement practices, prevention strategies, etc.) and (criminal) or justice (related to the response after a crime is committed, including penitentiary aspects) perspective. Exclusions: this indicator does not cover dialogues and processes of an operational nature (e.g., cooperation networks or working groups set up to discuss operational aspects). These will be reported under indicator OP1.1.3.

title.narrative: OP1.1.1. Number of regional and biregional cooperation strategies and/or agreements to fight organised crime designed, revised and/or ready to be implemented with the programmes support

description.narrative: The indicator will measure the number of cooperation strategies and/or agreements to fight organized crime designed or revised with the programme support, which are under implementation. Aside from regional and biregional, national (interinstitutional) strategies and agreements will also be considered.This indicator covers the following types of documents (they do not need to be binding): Strategies: documents adopted by one or more institutions which establish specific objectives or goals, develop a comprehensive plan or roadmap to achieve them and, often, allocate resources. Agreements: documents adopted by two or more institutions that establish a formal understanding or arrangement betweenthem. At the very least, they must reflect a commitment to cooperate and establish specific terms, conditions and obligations. In the context of combating organized crimes, agreements are generally used to establish the means and channels for cooperation and collaboration between different entities, covering aspects such as information sharing, mutual legal assistance, operational coordination, etc. A key example of an agreement would be a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).The documents need to make explicit reference to organized crime (as a whole or specific aspects of it, e.g., specific markets, types of counter operations). Exclusions: This indicator does not cover:a. Political declarations. Political declarations that are likely to lead to the adoption of strategies / agreements can be reported as progress (see below). b. Other types of strategic documents that do not set any objectives (e.g., reports identifying key threats). These are reported under OT1.1.2 (see below).c. Documents covering security / safety threats without an explicit reference to organized crime. These fall outside the mandate of EL PACCTO 2.0.d. Agreements between LAC institutions and EL PACCTO 2.0 (framework agreements). e. International / interinstitutional agreements for the creation of JITs, SMTs, etc. These will be reported under OT3. The indicator covers strategies/agreements that have been designed or revised, covering both new strategies / agreements and the amendment of existing strategies / agreements. For it to be reported as a result, the agreement / strategy needs to be effectively implemented by the relevant institution(s). All the steps towards that (document drafted, adopted, etc.) will be reported as progress (see Commentary, examples and/or limitations).

title.narrative: OP1.1.3. Number of individuals participating in national, regional, and international dialogues and awarenessraising events on organised crime

description.narrative: Dialogues and awareness raising events are events that seek to facilitate the dissemination and exchange of information and, ultimately, cooperation between two or more institutions. These can take the form of seminars, conferences, workshops, exercises, exchanges of information and best practices, networking events, etc. Note that only dialogues and events supported by EL PACCTO 2.0 (covering topics that are part of its mandate) will be considered. They can be recurrent or isolated events. They can be hosted in person or online.EL PAcCTOs active participation: EL PACCTOs support can imply that the programme is the organiser (or coorganiser) of the event or that it has an active participation (i.e., an EL PACCTO team member / expert delivers a presentation / leads a session on a specific topic covered by the programme (i.e., beyond presenting the programme). Relationship with other indicators: Dialogues and awarenessraising events that relate to the strategic and policy dialogue processes reported under indicator OT1.1.2 are also considered under this indicator as the two indicators are measuring different elements (number of processes vs number of participants). Exclusions: this indicator does not cover: Awarenessraising or exchange initiatives that do not have a specific, closed audience. For instance, a publication made available to several institutions cannot be considered under this indicator as it would not be possible to determine the number of individuals accessing it. Bilateral meetings between EL PACCTO 2.0 representatives and LAC institutions. Representatives from EL PACCTO 2.0 team as participants to the event, nor participants supporting the (logistical) implementation of the event (e.g., translators) or representing media organizations. This is to adequately reflect the actual reach of these events.

title.narrative: OP1.2.4. Number of technical and methodological training and/or regulatory frameworks designed, revised, and/or ready to be implemented with the support of the intervention

description.narrative: This indicator relates to activities in which EL PACCTO 2.0 provides technical assistance to institutions to support the design or revision of technical and methodological training frameworks, or regulatory frameworks that support general or specific aspects of the fight against organized crime. Technical and methodological training frameworks are the endresult of a process that identifies training needs and establishes how these should be filled, defining the training curriculum (content), delivery method and certification process. In this particular case, the trainings can seek to enhance methodological / technical skills directly related to operations or cover transversal / crosscutting topics (e.g., human rights, gender approaches, youth protection, victim protection, international cooperation and standards) that ultimately, ensure more effective and transparent procedures within the context of organized crime cases (including for the protection of victims and vulnerable individuals affected by organized crime). Technical and methodological regulatory frameworks refer to: a) sets of rules on specific technical and methodological aspects related to the investigation, prosecution, and protection of victims of organized crime cases (e.g., set up new procedures or tools that enhance the effectiveness and transparency of prevention and response efforts as well as interinstitutional and international cooperation, establish (common) methodologies, standards and tools, etc.), or b) guidance / instructions on technical and methodological processes related to the investigation, prosecution, and protection of victims of organized crime cases, e.g., how to set up SMTs (EMEs), JITs (ECIs) or GTIs, how to exchange information with other countries / institutions, etc. Overall, they refer to institutionalised practices or methodologies that determine how institutions function internally and/or engage with other stakeholders (e.g., the periodic and standarised sharing of information between government agencies within a given country or methodologies employed to analyse threats of organised crime or gather of evidence for investigations of particular types of crimes such as cybercrime or environmental crime). They may apply to specific criminal markets or crosscutting topics (e.g., human rights, gender approaches, youth protection, victim protection, international cooperation and standards). Other topics that may be covered are digitalization, data protection, etc.Under implementation means that the framework is fully designed / revised and has been officially adopted / circulated by the institution at hand. Exclusions: This indicator does not cover:a. Binding rules which do not cover specific technical / methodological aspects should not be considered under this indicator, but indicator OT1.2.3.b. Guidance on how to conduct operations, as this is covered under indicator OT1.2.5.

title.narrative: OP1.2.3. Number of national laws, policies, or other norms designed, revised and/or ready to be implemented with the support of the intervention

description.narrative: The indicator will quantify the number of national laws, policies, or other norms designed or, revised with the support of the intervention. National laws, policies and norms consist of binding, legislative or nonlegislative, documents adopted by government institutions in LAC countries for the purpose of countering organized crime (generally or focusing on specific criminal markets or aspects of the fight against organized crime). They may set up legislative requirements, establish specific objectives or lines of action, attribute roles and responsibilities, set up new /specialized institutions and/or units within existing institutions, national cooperation structures (e.g., networks, working groups, committees), etc. Laws, policies and other norms could be new or they could be adjusted, updated or developed with the support of the programme: Law: a formally recognised binding norm enforced by a controlling authority. In the context of the program, the criteria to consider that a norm is a law is the one established by each country. Norms: other norms reported under this indicator include regulation developed to enforce and develop the implementation of a given law or norms of higher hierarchy such, for example, constitutional ammendments. Policies: a comprehensive plan of action to structure the action of government institutions toward common goal or goals. The indicator specifically refers to laws, policies and norms designed or revised, covering both new laws / policies / norms as well as existing laws that were amended or modified (e.g., their content or scope of application revised). See `comments, assumptions and limitations for instructions on when they can be counted as a result.Exclusions: The creation of (regional and biregional) operational networks or mechanisms focused on specific criminal markets (similar to ARCO, LYNX, etc.) are not considered for this indicator, as they are covered under OT1.3.1.

title.narrative: OP1.3.4. Number of interinstitutional coordination mechanisms (Specialised Multidisciplinary Teams, Interinstitutional Technical Committees, or others) created and/or promoted with the support of the intervention

description.narrative: Interinstitutional coordination mechanisms cover operational or technical coordination mechanisms that involve representatives from different institutions / with different mandates, for the purpose of strengthening the fight against organized crime in key criminal markets (drugs, human, firearms and cultural goods trafficking and cyber and environmental crimes). Examples of such mechanisms include Specialised Multidisciplinary Teams (teams with clear rules on its objectives, scope, legal basis, organizational structure and principles of action that promote coordination and facilitate cooperation and information exchanges), Technical Committees (usually created to establish rules or standards), but they can also consist of multidisciplinary working groups, collaboration networks or platforms or other types of adhoc coordination mechanisms, as long as they involve institutions with different mandates. Mechanisms to facilitate information exchanges between different institutions should also be considered under this indicator: EMEs/SMTs: Equipos Multidisciplinarios Especializados Multidisciplinary Specialised Teams. EMEs involve stakeholders from at least two institutions (mainly police and justice institutions). Their objective is to conduct criminal investigations and operations on a specific topic. They are specialised and dedicated exclusively to the fight against a certain criminal phenomenon for example, environmental crimes. CTIs/Technical Committees: Comits Tcnicos Interinstitucionales Interinstitutional Technical Committees. CTIs involve stakehoders from at least two institutions from the same country. In the context of EL PAcCTO, they are institutions from the penal chain (police, justice or penitentiary) but might also include other stakeholders. For example, human rights bodies, Ministries of Foreign Affairs, instititutions promoting gender equality, or others. In some cases, they even involve civil society or academic institutions not only actors from the public sector. Their objective is to coordinate the action of different stakeholders towards the implementation of strategies to fight organised crime. For example, for the implementation of alternative measures to imprisionment through the coordination of pentientiary and justice institutions (Argentina, Colombia, Ecuador, Panam and Paraguay) or the improvement of international judicial cooperation via the collaboration of central autorities (Panam). Other: In some cases, partner institutions from Latin America already have interinstitutional mechanisms in place to strengthen the fight against organised crime. For example, Ecuador created an Interinstitutional Crisis Commission to adress its penitentiary crisis and Colombia and Uruguay have Criminal Policy Councils to inform policymaking on aspects relevant to the fight against organised crime. EL PAcCTO can and has contributed to the formalisation of these interinstitutional mechanisms and their functioning although they were not created with the programs support. However, they are still accounted for in this indicator because EL PAcCTO has contributed to their strengthtening. Promoted should be understood as strengthened.

title.narrative: OP1.3.5. Number of operational protocols, guidelines and/or regulations created or modified at the national and international level with the support of the intervention

description.narrative: Operational protocols, guidelines and/or regulations should be understood as binding (protocols and regulations) and nonbinding (guidelines) documents that set out instructions or specific steps that can be followed by stakeholders involved in the prosecution of these crimes. Unlike methodological and technical regulatory frameworks (see indicator OT1.2.4), the documents reported under this indicator are internal to the cooperation mechanisms / networks / teams reported covered by OT1.3. The documents can be, for instance, internal standard operating procedures or guidelines on how to conduct operations. As such, OT1.3.5 only covers operational protocols, guidelines and/or regulations related to the functioning or operations of specific (operational or technical) cooperation mechanisms (drugs, human, firearms and cultural goods trafficking and cyber and environmental crimes) (see Exclusions and links with other indicators for more information).The indicator covers protocols / guidelines / regulations created (i.e., they did not exist before and have been newly created under EL PACCTO 2.0) or modified (i.e., they existed they may or may not have been created during Phase I of EL PAcCTO but their content has been updated, refined, extended to other institutions/countries) during Phase II of the programme.

title.narrative: I3. Average overall Resilience Scores of LAC in the Organised Crime Index

description.narrative: This indicator measures the resilience score, as defined by the Organized Crime Index, in two regions (LAC and EU) and two LAC subregions (Latin America and Caribbean). The OCINDEX defines resilience as the ability to withstand and disrupt organized criminal activities as a whole, rather than individual markets, through political, economic, legal and social measures. Resilience refers to countries measures taken by both the state and nonstate actors.The OCINDEX Resilience indicator consists of 12 indicators constituting building blocks. The indicators are: Political leadership: States role in responding to organized crime and its effectiveness. Strong political leadership/governance suggests higher resilience. Government transparency and accountability: Degree to which states have put oversight mechanisms in place to ensure against state collusion in illicit activities. International cooperation: A countrys supranational structures and processes of interaction, policy making and concrete implementation to respond to organized crime. National policies and laws: A states legal action and structures put in place to respond to organized crime. Juidicial system and detention: A states judiciarys power to effectively and indepdently enforce judgements on organized crime and crimerelated cases. Law enforcement: A states ability to investigate, gather intelligence, protect and enforce adherence to its rules and procedures against organized crime. Territorial integrity: Degree to which states are able to control their physical and cyber territory and infrastructure against organized criminal activities. Antimoney laundering: A states ability to implement measures to combat money laundering and other related threats to the integrity of its financial system. Economic regulatory capacity: Ability to control/manage the economy and regulate transactions (national and international) for trade to thrive within the rule of law. Victim and witness support: Assistance provided to victims of various forms of organized crime, including initiatives such as witness protection programs. Prevention: Existence of strategies, measures, resource allocation, programmes and processes that are aimed at inhibiting organized crime. Nonstate actors: Degree nonstate actors are allowed to engage in OC responses and their roles in supporting State efforts /as watchdogs to governments.

description.narrative: The WJP Rule of Law Index defines rule of law as a durable system of laws, institutions, norms, and community commitment that delivers four universal principles: accountability, just law, open government, and accessible and impartial justice: Accountability: The government as well as private actors are accountable under the law. Just Law: The law is clear, publicized, and stable and is applied evenly. It ensures human rights as well as property, contract, and procedural rights. Open Government: The processes by which the law is adopted, administered, adjudicated, and enforced are accessible, fair, and efficient. Accessible and Impartial Justice: Justice is delivered timely by competent, ethical, and independent representatives and neutrals who are accessible, have adequate resources, and reflect the makeup of the communities they serve.The WJP Rule of Law indexcaptures adherence to the rule of law (as defined by the WJP as universal principles above) based on 9 factors: 1. Constraints on government power; 2. Absence of Corruption; 3. Open Government; 4. Fundamental Rights; 5. Order and Security; 6. Regulatory Enforcement; 7. Civil Justice; 8. Criminal Justice; 9. Informal Justice, further disaggregated into 47 specific subfactors.

title.narrative: I2. Average Criminal Market Scores in the Americas in the Organised Crime Index

description.narrative: The OCINDEX criminal market score measures the scope, scale and monetary and nonmonetary impact of 15 criminal markets (5 were added in the 2023 index), i.e., political, social and economic systems surrounding all stages of the illicit trade in and/or exploitation of commodities or people. The criminal markets are distributed across 4 areas and two crosscutting themes, and each market is reflected in an indicator: People: Human trafficking (CM1), Human smuggling (CM2) and Extortion and protection racketeering (CM3); Trade: Arms trafficking (CM4), Trade in counterfeit goods (CM5), Illicit trade in excisable goods (CM6); Environment: Flora crimes (CM7), Fauna crimes (CM8), Nonrenewable resource crimes (CM9); Drugs: Heroin trade (CM10), Cocaine trade (CM11), Cannabis trade (CM12) and Synthetic drug trade (CM13); Crosscutting themes: Cyberdependent crimes (CM14) and Financial crimes (CM15). For the purposes of Indicator I.2., the following criminal markets are selected: Drugs trafficking, which corresponds to the Drugs category under the OCINDEX (CM1013). As such, it covers the production, distribution and sale of heroin, cocaine and its derivatives and synthetic drugs. It also covers the illicit cultivation, distribution and sale of cannabis oil, resin, herbs or leaves. Consumption is considered in determining the reach of the criminal market. Human trafficking, which corresponds to the People category (CM12). It covers: the illicit activity involving coercion, deception, abduction or fraud for the purpose of exploitation, regardless of the victims consent (Human trafficking in the OCINDEX) but also activities by an organized crime group involving the illegal entry, transit or residence of migrants for a financial or material benefit (Human smuggling). Arms trafficking, which corresponds to indicator CM4 in the OCINDEX (Arms trafficking). This refers to the sale, acquisition, movement and diversion of arms, their parts and ammunition from legal to illegal commerce and/or across borders. Environmental crimes, which corresponds to the Environment category (CM79). This covers the illicit trade and possession of flora and fauna species (as well as their poaching in the latter case) covered by the CITES convention and other species covered under national law. Fauna crimes also includes IUU fishing. Nonrenewable resource crimes refers to the illicit extraction, smuggling, mingling, bunkering or mining of natural resources and the illicit trade of such commodities. Cybercrimes, which corresponds to Cyberdependent crimes (CM14), one of the two crosscutting themes. This includes organized crimes that rely solely on using information communications technology with the aim of obtaining a monetary/material benefit.
